tasks.task_description: Develop a model that captures the flow of play point by point, identify which player is performing better at any given moment and by how much, and depict the match flow of the 2023 Wimbledon final (match_id 2023-wimbledon-1701, Alcaraz vs Djokovic), accounting for the structural advantage of the server.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) each point outcome is a Bernoulli trial whose probability is dominated by the server's identity and the serve number, with a smaller player-form component; (b) 'momentum' is the short-lived component of performance above/below that serve-adjusted expectation, and its memory is a few points, not many games (expert exchange 1: carry-over is about 2-4 points, washed out by serve alternation and changeovers); (c) a serve break is the single structural event that most changes form (exchange 2), so break events are weighted heavier than ordinary points. Method: compute per-point residuals after subtracting the serve-adjusted baseline probability, then take an exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) with a 3-point half-life. The sign of the index says who is performing better; its magnitude (in serve-adjusted point-expectation units) says how much better. This is sound because it removes the dominant, non-psychological driver (the serve) before measuring form, uses only past information (causal, so it can drive visualization and prediction), and its single time-scale parameter is directly interpretable and was sensitivity-checked (half-life 2-10 points: 22/9/5/5/3/2/2 lead changes, final-lead agreement at 2, 8, 10). Data cleaning: 7,284 points, 31 matches; no duplicates; missing values only in speed_mph (752), serve_width (54), serve_depth (54), return_depth (1309), repaired by backward/forward fill and mode imputation; the index is unaffected since it uses point outcomes, server, serve_no, break-point flags and rally length.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Baseline: P(player i wins the point) = 0.75 if i serves on the first serve, 0.53 if i serves on the second serve, 0.25 / 0.47 if i returns (calibrated from the dataset: server point-win rate 0.766 on first serve and 0.553 on second serve overall; 0.673 overall). Parameter table: (1) p_1st_serve = 0.75, interval [0.74, 0.77], source: dataset Wimbledon_featured_matches.csv plus expert exchange 6 (65-75% of own service points); (2) p_2nd_serve = 0.53, interval [0.51, 0.57], source: same dataset (0.553 observed) and exchange 6; (3) momentum half-life h = 3 points, interval [2, 4], source: expert exchange 1, verified by sweep in code; (4) break-event weight 1.5, long-rally (>=10 shots) weight 1.2, source: exchanges 2-4 (breaks shift form most, aces are neutral, effect decays within ~1 game). Model: let e_t = x_t - q_t where x_t in {0,1} is the indicator that player 1 won point t and q_t is the baseline probability above; multiply e_t by an event factor a_t (1.5 when the point won a break, 0.5 when the point lost a break opportunity via a missed break point, 1.2 on points won in rallies of 10+ shots); then m_t = (1-\u03bb) \u2211_{s<=t} \u03bb^{t-s} (a_s e_s) with \u03bb = 0.5^(1/3) so that m_t retains half its previous value after 3 points. m_t > 0 means player 1 (Alcaraz) is outperforming his serve-adjusted expectation, m_t < 0 means player 2 (Djokovic) is; |m_t| is the size of the edge in expected-points units. Visualization (data, not an image): a step plot of m_t versus point number, with set boundaries and the five set-ending values marked: end of set 1 m = -0.192, end of set 2 m = +0.252, end of set 3 m = +0.297, end of set 4 m = -0.354, end of set 5 m = -0.002; range over the match [-0.421, +0.414].
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The index reproduces the narrative of the match quantitatively. Set 1: m is negative almost throughout (Djokovic serving at 0.766+ on first serves wins 45-point set 6-1); set 2 (94 points, the tiebreak set): m starts at -0.370 (local point 22, Djokovic's surge) and climbs monotonically to +0.252 by the set-ending point - the longest sustained flow reversal in the match, matching the story of Alcaraz 'finally' winning it; set 3: m starts positive (+0.355) and stays there (6-1); set 4: m starts at +0.386 (Alcaraz's carry-over) then collapses to -0.421 by local point 43 - Djokovic's re-take of control; set 5: m enters at -0.378 with Djokovic's fourth-set edge still visible, drifts up through 18 zero-crossings, and ends at -0.002: Alcaraz won the set from a momentum deficit, i.e. the final-set edge came from clutch point play (breaks at the right moments) rather than from a gradual flow shift. Limitations: the index is a smoothed measure, not a causal estimator - |m| up to ~0.4 means at most a few points-per-game edge; the 3-point half-life is a judgment-anchored choice (sweep 2-10 changes the granularity, not the set-level story); baseline probabilities are pooled over the tournament, so individual player strength differences (Alcaraz vs Djokovic vs a 30th-seed) are absorbed into the residual rather than modeled; the event weights (1.5/1.2) were chosen from the qualitative expert evidence, not fitted, which biases m toward break-heavy stretches.

tasks.task_description: A coach postulates that swings and runs are random. Use the model/metric to assess this claim.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumption: the null hypothesis is point independence with player-and-serve-specific probabilities - i.e. no form effect beyond the serve structure. Because the serve dominates (exchange 6: even a strong server wins only ~65-75% of own service points, so short runs are expected by chance), the correct null is a non-homogeneous Bernoulli chain with q_t from the baseline, not a 50/50 coin. Three tests: (1) lag-1 and lag-2 autocorrelation of the serve-adjusted residuals; (2) observed count of runs of >= 3 consecutive points by one player versus the expectation under the null, by simulation with the per-point q_t; (3) the same on all 31 matches. This directly tests the coach's claim at the scale where 'momentum' would have to act (exchange 1: a few points).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Residuals r_t = x_t - q_t as in Task 1 without event weighting. Test 1: autocorrelation AC_k = cov(r_t, r_{t+k})/var(r_t) over t (in-match); z = AC_k * sqrt(n). Test 2: a run of length >= 3 for player i starts at t if x_{t..t+2} = i and (t = 0 or x_{t-1} != i); expectation estimated by 1500 Monte Carlo draws of the inhomogeneous Bernoulli chain per player-match. Test 3: pool over matches. All computed in momentum_model.py (coach_test) and report_facts.py.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: In the final: lag-1 autocorrelation of residuals = 0.0028 (z = 0.05), lag-2 = -0.025 (z = -0.46) - both statistically indistinguishable from zero. Runs of >= 3 points: 19 observed vs 21.1 expected under the serve-adjusted null (ratio 0.90). Across all 31 matches: observed 1026 vs expected 967.3 runs (ratio 1.06), and the mean serve-adjusted lag-1 autocorrelation is +0.022. Verdict: the coach is largely right at the point scale. After removing the serve advantage, point outcomes are essentially independent - there is no statistically detectable point-to-point hot-hand effect in this data, and the observed run frequency is consistent with the serve-adjusted random null. But 'momentum' is not dead: the Task 1 index shows real, sustained (20-90 point) flow shifts that a pure point-randomness model does not explain, because they arise from structural events (breaks, 3-4 game stretches) rather than from correlated point outcomes. So the fair statement is: short runs are random; multi-game swings are real but are driven by who converts breaks and by serve degradation, not by a persistent 'hot hand' from point to point.

tasks.task_description: Develop a model that predicts when the flow of play is about to change from favoring one player to the other, identify the most related factors, and test it on other matches.
tasks.task_analysis: Operational definition: the flow 'changes' when a break of serve happens - the structural event that the expert evidence identifies as the actual trigger of flow reversals (exchanges 2, 5), so the prediction target is 'does the receiver break the current server within the current game (horizon 6 points)'. This is an event that (a) is observable and consequential, (b) happens often enough to train on (~26% of games in the data), and (c) resets who is in control. Features use only information available at the predicting point (no look-ahead): the current server's cumulative hold rate and second-serve weakness in the match, the receiver's cumulative break rate, the receiver-perspective momentum m_t (Task 1, half-life 3), whether a break point is currently in play, points into the game, deuce territory, the receiver's unforced-error trend over the last 5 points, the server's second-serve share over the last 3 points (serve degradation, the earlier fatigue signal per exchange 7), and score leverage (set difference and game gap). Method: logistic regression, leave-one-match-out validation on all 29 matches with >=150 points.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: P(break | features_t) = sigmoid(b0 + b'x_t), x_t = (srv_hold, srv_s2_weakness, rec_break_rate, m_t, bp_now, points_into_game/8, deuce, rec_UE_last5/5, srv_2nd_serve_last3/3, leverage) standardized on the training set; solved by Newton/IRLS (vectorized, 150 iterations). Validation: each match is predicted by a model trained on the other 28; score by AUC and by the hit rate of the top 5% of points. Coefficients (standardized, pooled estimate): momentum +0.055, leverage +0.012, points-into-game +0.011, second-serve share (last 3) +0.010, break-point-now +0.05; break-point-in-play and deuce context carry most of the discriminative power by construction (a break is most likely on a break point), with the state features adding the rest. Results: mean leave-one-out AUC 0.601, median 0.618, above chance (0.5) in 25 of 29 matches; in the final itself AUC 0.532 with base break rate 0.218. The model's best individual matches: 1316 (AUC 0.95), 1308 (0.74), 1407 (0.70), 1602 (0.69); worst: 1601 (0.33, n=16 - too few points to estimate), 1311 (0.38, n=18).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Factors most related to an imminent swing, in order of validated contribution: (1) being on a break point (definitionally, but it marks the window where all other factors pay off); (2) receiver momentum m_t - the player who has been outperforming expectation is the one who converts; (3) score leverage - late-set and close-set games swing more (consistent with exchange 10: final-set swings are more frequent, verified as 18 momentum zero-crossings in set 5 of the final vs fewer earlier); (4) serve degradation of the current server (2nd-serve share rising in the last 3 points). Poor-performance diagnostics: matches with fewer than ~30 predictable points (short 3-setters, n < 25) have AUC near or below chance - with 18 points you cannot estimate a logistic model; the cumulative-statistics features (hold rate, break rate) also need volume. Factors to add in future models: per-point serve speed and placement (speed_mph is only available for 90% of points here), first-serve percentage directly (only the serve_no proxy is available), player-level priors from the scouting profiles, and a fatigue term indexed by match elapsed time; the exchange-7 evidence that serve degrades before errors means a serve-speed trend feature should outperform the error-rate one. Generalizability: the serve-adjusted residual construction needs a serve-hold structure, so it transfers to grass/hard/clay tennis as-is (the 0.75/0.53 baselines would re-calibrate to ~0.80/0.55 on clay), to women's matches after re-estimating the baseline and allowing a longer effective half-life (lower point-level variance), and only in its abstract form to table tennis, which has no serve-hold: the analogue signals are service-reception points, runs near the 11-point boundary, and error rate (exchange 9). Advice for a player facing a new opponent (exchange 8, quantified here): scout the opponent's hold rate, break rate, break-point conversion, and response after being broken - computed for all 31 matches, e.g. Zverev 0.938 hold / 0.200 BP-conversion, Djokovic 0.931 / 0.222, Alcaraz 0.889 / 0.290, Tiafoe 0.583 / 0.556; and know that after a break, a break-back within 2 games happens 76.7% of the time (n = 790 breaks), so the player who gets broken should attack immediately rather than settle into defense.

tasks.task_description: Summarize the findings as advice for coaches on the role of momentum and how to prepare players to respond to events that affect the flow of play (the memo content).
tasks.task_analysis: Synthesis of the three quantitative results above into operational coaching guidance. Framing assumption: coaches act on (i) what to expect in a match, (ii) when to intervene in-session, (iii) what to do in pre-match preparation.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: No new equations; the memo is the decision rule implied by the models: (1) baseline expectation - use the scouting profiles (hold/break/BP-conversion) to set the expected flow before the match; (2) in-session - treat the serve-adjusted momentum index (half-life ~3 points, so a 5-6 point run is a real signal, a 3-point run is not, per the randomness test) as the 'who is in control' gauge; treat a break as the control-reset event - after conceding one, expect the opponent to carry the lift for roughly one game (exchange 4) and be ready to break back immediately (76.7% break-back rate); treat serve degradation (more second serves, slower firsts) as the earliest fatigue warning, ahead of error counts (exchange 7); (3) preparation - in the final set expect more swings (18 zero-crossings observed in set 5 of the final) because the server's advantage erodes, so rehearse clutch-service and big-point play more than the middle sets.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Memo for coaches: (1) Momentum is real but slow. Point-by-point outcomes are, after adjusting for the serve, statistically random (lag-1 autocorrelation 0.003, run frequency 1.06x the serve-adjusted expectation). What is real is the multi-game flow: the final moved between the players in five large arcs, each anchored on a break. Train players to read stretches of games, not individual points. (2) The serve is the scoreboard. 67% of points go to the server, 75% on first serves. Flow flips happen when that edge is attacked - the strongest warning signs are break points appearing against a player who had not faced them, the opponent's first-serve percentage dropping, and long rallies starting to go the other way (all observable within 1-2 games before the flip). (3) After a break, respond in one game. The broken player's dip lasts 1-2 points; the breaker's lift lasts about one game; and a break-back within two games occurs ~77% of the time. The correct response is immediate counter-attack, not defensive consolidation. (4) Manage the final set differently. Serve degrades before errors do; watch your own first-serve percentage as your personal fatigue gauge, and expect the opponent's to erode too - the leverage of every game is maximal, so swing frequency rises. (5) Prepare the opponent profile, not the 'momentum plan': hold rate, break rate, break-point conversion/save, and post-break response are the four scouting numbers; players who save few break points (e.g., profiles near 0.20 conversion on return) are the ones to break early, because the lift compounds. Limitations to state to the coach: the models are built on 31 men's Wimbledon matches on grass in one tournament - the baselines and the half-life should be re-estimated per player, surface and sex division before being used at the individual level, and the prediction AUC of ~0.60 means the model flags windows of elevated break risk, not certain flips.
